items.questionAndWhy: Does an AI that appears to understand a person socially become more influential even when its advice is wrong? The question distinguishes interpersonal rapport from evidence of accuracy.
items.whatTheyDid: In a randomized study, 462 working adults with recent AI experience received either a high-social-intelligence relational framing package or a neutral AI. Over six repeated decision trials, researchers measured advice-taking and post-interaction judgments of trust and verification.
items.whatTheyFound: The relational package increased advice-taking both when initially correct participants received wrong AI advice (odds ratio 1.507) and when initially incorrect participants received correct advice (odds ratio 1.800). The difference between those effects was not significant. Advice correctness depended on initial participant accuracy, not a separately randomized accuracy manipulation.
items.whatItMeans: Socially responsive interfaces may increase acceptance of advice without improving users' discrimination between correct and incorrect recommendations. In PSYWERX human–AI evaluations, measure harmful overrides separately from beneficial corrections. The proposed social-to-epistemic pathway is not causally established by the post-interaction associations.
items.streamTitle: Relationally persuasive AI increased both helpful reliance and harmful overreliance
items.streamSummary: A randomized 462-adult study found relational AI framing increased reliance on both correct and incorrect advice. Accuracy sensitivity and the proposed trust mechanism remain unproven.
items.attribution: Mizrak, Kirgiz and Demirel — Journal of Intelligence (randomized experiment)

items.questionAndWhy: Do engagement-optimized feeds distort perceptions of political discourse, and can alternative ranking rules reduce that distortion without making the feed less enjoyable?
items.whatTheyDid: A registered report randomized 2,000 participants to custom social-media feed algorithms for eight weeks around the 2024 US presidential election. The conditions included engagement-based, reverse-chronological and diversified-extremity ranking, with measures of exposure, perceived norms, partisan animosity, engagement and enjoyment.
items.whatTheyFound: Engagement-based ranking increased exposure to intergroup, moralized, emotional and toxic content, reduced the accuracy of prescriptive social-norm perceptions in an unexpected direction, and increased perceived partisan animosity. It did not significantly change participants' own engagement behavior. Diversified-extremity ranking improved norm accuracy and reduced problematic exposure while maintaining similar enjoyment.
items.whatItMeans: Feed design changes what users infer about the political environment, even where their measurable engagement remains unchanged. PSYWERX assessments should separate exposure, norm perceptions and actual activity. This strong older field experiment is newly useful during the November 2026 election; effects in other platforms and election cycles require replication.
items.streamTitle: Eight-week election-feed experiment altered norm perceptions without reliably changing engagement
items.streamSummary: In an eight-week randomized study of 2,000 users, engagement ranking worsened political norm perceptions; diversified ranking improved them without reducing enjoyment. Participants' own engagement did not significantly change.
items.attribution: Brady et al. — Nature (registered randomized feed experiment)

items.questionAndWhy: Does the mind represent different kinds of complexity using a common dimension, or are visual, auditory and symbolic complexity unrelated judgments?
items.whatTheyDid: Eleven behavioral experiments involving 1,500 participants tested reward transfer and judgments across shapes, dot arrays, melodies, letter strings, mathematical expressions and tactile forms. They also examined whether complexity judgments carried over into irrelevant tasks and aesthetic preferences.
items.whatTheyFound: Learning about complexity transferred across stimulus classes. Task-irrelevant complexity affected later judgments, and individual differences in preference for complexity showed similarities across domains. The experiments support a shared representational component but do not demonstrate that all real-world information has one measurable psychological complexity value.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX communication and training research, message complexity might be measured across formats rather than treating every medium independently. This remains a hypothesis for complex political or operational material; the tests involved controlled stimuli rather than field comprehension or persuasion.
items.streamTitle: Complexity judgments generalized across vision, sound, language and touch
items.streamSummary: Eleven experiments (N=1,500) found cross-modal transfer of complexity judgments across visual, auditory, symbolic and tactile stimuli. Application to complex messages is untested.
items.attribution: Boger and Firestone — Nature Human Behaviour (11 behavioral experiments)

items.questionAndWhy: How can real administrative failures and unrelated visual evidence be recast as claims of election interference before verification catches up?
items.whatTheyDid: On November 3, Associated Press reporters checked circulating claims against election officials, statements from the FBI, and the origins of accompanying images. Cases included a ballot-scanner programming problem in Westchester County, a supposed Houston FBI ballot raid, misleading imagery and false texts about polling-place changes.
items.whatTheyFound: The Westchester scanner failure was real, but AP found no credible evidence it was deliberately engineered to suppress votes. The FBI explicitly denied the alleged Houston raid; accompanying images came from unrelated events. Fulton County reported false polling-place texts, while sender identity and intent remained unknown. The article did not measure claim reach or changed votes.
items.whatItMeans: A PSYWERX information-integrity assessment should separate the triggering event, asserted explanation, evidence provenance, attribution and measured audience effects. Contemporaneous corrections are operationally relevant, but occurrence of rumors is not proof of a coordinated campaign or electoral impact.
items.streamTitle: Election Day glitches and unrelated images were rapidly turned into unverified fraud narratives
items.streamSummary: AP's November 3 case checks separated a genuine New York scanner fault from unverified sabotage claims, disproved a Houston ballot-raid rumor and documented false Georgia polling texts of unknown origin.
items.attribution: Melissa Goldin and Calvin Woodward — Associated Press (original Election Day fact checks)

items.questionAndWhy: How should military and civilian activities be synchronized across domains to generate effects and preserve decisions when communications or technology are degraded?
items.whatTheyDid: NATO Allied Command Transformation reported on the October 2026 Multi-Domain Operations Conference in Split, Croatia, with more than 200 participants from 30 nations. Discussions addressed cyber and space integration, coordination across domains, civil–military synchronization and digital transformation, including wargaming and exercises.
items.whatTheyFound: The November 3 account documents four priorities and the ambition to be fully multi-domain-operations enabled by 2030. It emphasizes operating through degraded networks and developing cross-domain command concepts. It does not provide independently measured gains in decision quality, deterrence, synchronization or battlefield outcomes.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX operational modeling, multi-domain synchronization needs explicit action-to-effect chains, cross-actor dependencies, decision latency and degraded-information tests. The NATO statement supplies practitioner requirements and activities, not validation of an effective capability.
items.streamTitle: NATO outlined a cross-domain synchronization problem, not a measured capability gain
items.streamSummary: NATO ACT's November 3 report describes four priorities for military–civilian multi-domain coordination across 30 nations. The conference was an implementation forum, not an evaluated improvement in operational effects.
items.attribution: NATO Allied Command Transformation — November 3 official conference report

items.questionAndWhy: Do AI agents delegated professional judgments respond to peers, superiors and client pressure like human professionals, or do their failures follow different patterns?
items.whatTheyDid: A preprint tested twelve LLM model settings acting as an audit senior associate. After each agent formed an analytical estimate, it received challenges without new evidence from an engagement partner, peers, an external-firm reviewer or a client's CFO, sometimes with an explicit career inducement.
items.whatTheyFound: Agents revised judgments under pressure from partners, peers and external reviewers in several settings, but generally not under CFO pressure. Career inducements often reduced rather than increased revision; some models revised only toward conservative estimates. These are controlled agent responses, not observed human auditors' behavior.
items.whatItMeans: Institutional roles and authority cues can alter AI-system outputs even without new evidence, but the profile of susceptibility is model-dependent and should not be mapped onto human compliance. PSYWERX research agents need role-pressure and evidence-free challenge tests along with independent human review.
items.streamTitle: Audit-task LLM agents yielded to some professional pressure but resisted a client inducement
items.streamSummary: Across twelve LLM audit settings, professional authority cues shifted some agent judgments without new evidence, while client career inducements often reduced revision. The behavior is not validated as human conformity.
items.attribution: Richard Zhe Wang — arXiv preprint (delegated-audit agent experiment)

items.questionAndWhy: When an agent improves its prompts, memory, tools or middleware, does it retain its old abilities and transfer improvements to unseen tasks?
items.whatTheyDid: SEAGym created separate frozen-validation, in-distribution, out-of-distribution, replay and cost views for evolving agent harnesses. The authors compared ACE, TF-GRPO and AHE over Terminal-Bench 2.0 and HLE tasks, saving intermediate harness snapshots and verified execution outcomes.
items.whatTheyFound: Validation gains did not always transfer to unseen tasks. One intermediate AHE snapshot fell to just 6 of 80 replay tasks solved because middleware changes caused execution errors; final scores alone would obscure this temporary breakdown. These results concern the tested benchmarks and agent backends.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX research pipelines, every agent change should be checked on untouched tasks, old successful cases, out-of-domain workflows and failure costs. The approach validates an evaluation methodology rather than any human behavioral model. Included for a specific reproducibility advance despite its June publication date.
items.streamTitle: Self-evolving agent evaluations caught regressions hidden by final benchmark scores
items.streamSummary: SEAGym separated agent-harness validation, held-out transfer and replay. An intermediate snapshot collapsed to 6/80 solved tasks, revealing a regression that final scores hid.
items.attribution: Zheng et al. — arXiv preprint (SEAGym agent evaluation)

items.questionAndWhy: Can simulation separate household decisions from financial-state updates and preserve heterogeneous responses over multiple time steps at very large scale?
items.whatTheyDid: S²-MAS described an engine with 500 million survey-grounded synthetic household personas, a compact financial-choice model trained on 2.93 million examples, and explicit ledgers for cash, debt, consumption and repayment. The authors simulated 12 million households in paired scenarios and a 24-month panel.
items.whatTheyFound: The decision model scored 74.55% accuracy but only 38.37% question-macro F1 on the reported tasks. Simulated purchases, deferrals and debt paths differed by household characteristics as purchase goals and credit conditions changed. These differences are outputs of the synthetic system; they do not independently establish accurate real-world policy effects.
items.whatItMeans: The transferable design is to keep action-choice models separate from state propagation and preserve household-specific histories. PSYWERX COA models could adopt that architecture, but population size is not evidence of behavioral fidelity; intervention forecasts still need independent human-data calibration and prospective tests.
items.streamTitle: A 500-million-persona synthetic economy emphasized the gap between scale and behavioral validity
items.streamSummary: S²-MAS reported 500 million synthetic household personas and 12 million simulated agents, with explicit decision/state separation. Its model's 38.37% macro F1 and absence of prospective policy tests constrain behavioral claims.
items.attribution: Li et al. — arXiv preprint (survey-grounded economic multi-agent framework)

items.questionAndWhy: How does representing group conversations rather than only person-to-person links change modeled opinion convergence and polarization?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers proposed a continuous-time opinion-dynamics system on hypergraphs, representing interactions among groups of nodes rather than only pairs. They analyzed mathematical stability and convergence with and without stubborn actors, followed by numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world network datasets.
items.whatTheyFound: The model generated different convergence and polarization patterns depending on higher-order interactions and stubborn-node assumptions. Its theoretical results and simulations evaluate formal dynamics; using a real network structure does not mean actual human opinion changes were measured or forecast prospectively.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX audience modeling, meetings, group chats and communities may require group-level interaction structures. Hypergraph variants could be compared against pairwise FCM or network models using observed longitudinal behavior. The value of the formalism for specific COAs remains untested.
items.streamTitle: Higher-order opinion model represented group interactions beyond pairwise social ties
items.streamSummary: An IEEE model replaces purely pairwise opinion links with group-level hypergraph interactions and derives convergence properties. Its simulated dynamics are not validated human intervention forecasts.
items.attribution: IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics: Systems — formal opinion-dynamics study

items.questionAndWhy: Can gaze traces reveal how people inspect stereoscopic network diagrams and guide changes to VR interfaces that improve analytical accuracy?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers ran a series of eye-tracking studies on single- and multi-layer stereoscopic 3D graphs in VR. They compared gaze exploration strategies, task performance and the effects of graph layout, then derived targeted visual cues from successful analysts' viewing patterns and tested them in a follow-up.
items.whatTheyFound: Gaze patterns varied with task and graph complexity. The gaze-derived cues improved task correctness in a majority of reported follow-up trials, although the abstract does not establish benefits for every task or provide operational field-validation evidence.
items.whatItMeans: The concrete PSYWERX-relevant affordance is instrumenting immersive causal or social-network displays to improve navigation and interpretation of complex relationships. Training and operational benefits remain untested; gaze association does not by itself reveal the correct psychological interpretation of a graph.
items.streamTitle: Eye-tracking-informed cues improved some immersive 3D network-analysis judgments
items.streamSummary: A 2026 IEEE paper used VR eye tracking to study 3D network analysis and derive visual cues that improved correctness in most follow-up trials. Real-world analytic transfer remains untested.
items.attribution: Wang et al. — IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (VR eye-tracking studies)
